title: The viewpoint pause: sit somewhere high before you decide
description: There is a reason people climb hills to think. A wide view measurably loosens a stuck mind — and you can borrow the effect with nothing more than a bench, a view and twenty unhurried minutes.

body.heading: Why the view does the work
paragraphs: Researchers who study attention describe natural scenes as 'softly fascinating': a valley, moving water, drifting cloud holds the eye without demanding anything from it. While that gentle attention rests, the effortful, list-making kind recovers — which is why a problem carried up a hill often feels smaller on the way down.

Height adds its own effect. From a viewpoint, your worries quite literally shrink to scale: the town where the difficult meeting happens becomes one rooftop among hundreds, and the brain seems to take the hint.

body.heading: How to take a viewpoint pause
paragraphs: Choose the highest, widest view you can reach easily — a hill bench, a top-floor window, a bridge, even a tall car park at quiet hours. Bring the one question you are stuck on, written on paper, and leave your phone in your pocket for the first ten minutes.

Read the question once, then look at the view and let your mind wander where it wants. The answer, if one comes, usually arrives sideways — a reordering of what matters rather than a bolt of genius. Write down whatever shifted before you head back down.

body.heading: Small enough to use weekly
paragraphs: This is not a retreat or a holiday; it is twenty minutes. People who build a small weekly pause into their routine often find they stop needing the emergency version — the frantic midnight worry session — quite so often.
Your thinking has a posture, just like your body. Sometimes the most productive thing you can do for a decision is change the view it is being made from.

takeaway: Take one written question to the widest view you can reach, give it twenty phone-free minutes, and write down what shifted before you leave.
